content: The first reported case of leishmaniasis co-infection with HIV occurred in 1985 in European Mediterranean countries. Since then, 35 countries, representing over one-third of endemic regions, have documented cases of co-infection due to the overlapping spread of these two diseases. Globally, 5-6% of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and HIV co-infection cases occur in the Mediterranean region. In certain areas of Ethiopia, up to 35% of leishmaniasis patients are co-infected with HIV, and this trend is expanding to neighboring countries like Sudan. In 2018, 75% of reported cases to the Ministry of Health were co-infections, compared to 5% in 2012. HIV and leishmaniasis are mutually exacerbating conditions, each worsening the other’s clinical course. HIV infection increases the risk of developing VL by 100 to 2,320 times in endemic areas. VL in co-infected patients is incurable, and those with CD4+ counts below 200 cells/μl experience frequent relapses, eventually becoming unresponsive to all available treatments. These patients carry a high parasite load and are highly infectious to sandflies, contributing to the spread of the disease. Treatment options for VL are limited due to the high cost, lack of drug registration, and toxicity of available antileishmanial medications. Many of these drugs are produced by single manufacturers, further complicating access. Additionally, there is no vaccine to prevent leishmania infection, making disease control reliant on access to diagnostic and treatment services. Treatment regimens for VL vary depending on the species of leishmania parasite and the eco-epidemiological region, leading to differing recommendations by the World Health Organization (WHO). The treatment of leishmaniasis in HIV-infected patients is particularly challenging due to reduced therapeutic options. Factors such as drug prices, lack of registration, toxicity, and untested efficacy in co-infected patients limit accessibility. Most evidence on treatment efficacy comes from European Mediterranean countries, where Leishmania infantum is the causative agent. This species differs in virulence and drug susceptibility compared to Leishmania donovani in Africa and Asia, where treatment efficacy has been less robust. Few studies have evaluated treatment efficacy outside the Mediterranean region, leaving optimal treatment regimens for East Africa and South-East Asia undefined. Currently, the standard therapy for VL in co-infected patients, as recommended by the WHO, involves intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 3-5 mg/kg daily or intermittently for 10 doses, totaling 40 mg/kg. Recent trials suggest that combining intravenous amphotericin B with oral miltefosine may be more effective. This highlights the need to revise WHO treatment recommendations for East African and South-East Asian settings, where the burden of VL-HIV co-infection is highest. The aim of this systematic review is to provide evidence to the WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) to update recommendations on combination therapy for VL in co-infected patients. The review seeks to answer two key questions: (1) What is the efficacy and safety of combination therapy with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and oral miltefosine compared to monotherapy with liposomal amphotericin B in East Africa and South-East Asia? (2) What is the efficacy and safety of secondary prophylaxis compared to no secondary prophylaxis after the first episode of VL in co-infected patients? The review included all comparative study designs, such as randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-RCTs, controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time-series studies, and case-control studies. Observational studies without control groups, such as single-arm cohorts and case series, were excluded from the main analysis but tabulated for completeness. Case reports with five or fewer participants were excluded. Contextual factors, including preferences, values, resource use, equity, acceptability, and feasibility, were assessed using studies of any design except case reports. The population of interest included individuals of all age groups diagnosed with HIV and co-infection with VL. Studies involving indirect populations, such as HIV-negative individuals with VL or populations outside East Africa and South-East Asia, were excluded. The interventions evaluated included combination therapy of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and oral miltefosine for VL in HIV-positive patients in East Africa and South-East Asia. The comparator was monotherapy with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B. Outcomes assessed included all-cause mortality, clinical cure at treatment completion and six months post-treatment, relapse (defined as recurrence of disease after successful treatment), adverse events, and patient satisfaction. Relapse was considered the most critical indicator of treatment efficacy and improved immunity. The systematic review involved an electronic search of databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, Medline, and Embase, with no restrictions on date, publication status, or language. Additional unpublished data and references were screened for inclusion. A total of 887 references were identified, and after screening, nine references (five studies) were included in the review. The review used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence and create a summary of findings. Certainty of evidence was downgraded for reasons such as study design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias. The evidence-to-decision framework facilitated the development of recommendations, considering factors such as desirable and undesirable effects, resource use, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. In conclusion, the systematic review aims to provide evidence to update WHO recommendations on combination therapy for VL-HIV co-infected patients, particularly in East Africa and South-East Asia, where the burden is highest.
